newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices jump on supply blockage in Venezuela.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices jump on supply blockage in Venezuela.

text.p: Oil prices gained on Tuesday after a grounded dredger blocked Venezuela's main crude export route, proving markets were still vulnerable to supply disruptions.

The dredger Catatumbo became grounded in the middle of the Lake Maracaibo shipping lane on Monday, completely halting traffic in the channel which normally exports more than one million barrels of crude a day.
Tugs were trying to refloat the dredger on Tuesday.
Oil futures in both London and New York jumped on the news, with benchmark Brent for October ending 14 cents up on the day at $19.07 a barrel.

The Maracaibo channel has become so heavily silted that the port has cut the maximum draught allowed through by some two feet (60 cm), reducing the amount of oil each tanker can carry by 70,000 barrels.
In February the Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos went aground in the same spot as the Catatumbo, spilling 25,000 barrels of oil.

"Demand is still strong at the moment and production is only just covering it," said Leslie Nicholas, analyst at brokers GNI in London, "so this sort of disruption is perfect for a short-term move up."
But without some idea of how long the blockage will last the market will not break out of its current technical limits, Nicholas added.
With Venezuela a big supplier of the lighter crudes needed to make gasoline, and the United States still consuming peak summer quantities of motor fuel, the blockage has occured at a vulnerable time.
But traders have begun to look towards the Northern Hemisphere autumn when gasoline demand will fall and heating oil output for the winter will rise.

The indecision over when the market outlook will change has left markets nervous, traders said, with many looking forward to U.S. industry stock data due later on Tuesday from the American Petroleum Institute (API).
The API figures will indicate if logistical problems with delivery of South American grades have greatly affected supply and if summer demand remains strong.
Preliminary soundings among brokers suggested gasoline stocks would show their eighth consecutive decline, yet another bullish sign.
The strength in U.S. gasoline demand has allowed world oil markets to shrug off the effect of resumed Iraqi exports.
Some 30 million barrels of Iraqi oil will be loaded at the Turkish port of Ceyhan and the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr in August, but look set to be absorbed without problems.
